The Map

Every word you keep hearing has a shape. A seat is a model. A pin is a rule saying which seat runs a job. A lane is a named job. The harness is omO itself — the thing that reads the pins and hands each job to a seat. A probe is the question "are you still there?" asked of a seat every few minutes. The board is the Estate page, which reads all of it. Tap any block on the canvas, or open a card below.

The console, face by face

Six faces, one nav row, and what each is for. Read off the running console on 2 October 2026.

Chattalk here

Where you talk to me. I do the work, delegate what needs delegating, and hand the result back as something you can look at.

  • Beside shows a page to the right of the chat; Open gives it its own window.
  • Chats lists past conversations, Stop halts me mid-turn, New chat starts fresh.
  • Name a page like /map in my reply and it arrives as a chip you tap to open beside the chat.
Estatethe live board

One surface for the whole system: which seat is on which lane, what the checks say, what it cost, and what needs your attention.

  • Checks — health (the hourly gate), self-check, tidy-check.
  • Lanes — which model runs which kind of work, live from the pins.
  • Findings — Safety, Drift and Idle: the things worth a look.
Mapthe vocabulary

This page. The words you keep hearing — seat, pin, lane, probe, harness — as one connected diagram, each block tappable, each card explaining it in plain language.

  • Deliberately not live: it cannot go stale or lie to you.
  • Grows one block at a time as the vocabulary does.
Sessionsevery conversation

Every open agent session, newest first, with the folder it belongs to, the model it is on, and whether it is busy.

  • Tap any row to come back to that conversation.
  • Use it instead of hunting through Zed's thread list.
Dropphone to Mac

Send a note, photo or file from your phone; it lands in the Mac's drop folder.

  • The fastest way to get something in front of me.
  • Needs the console token on the phone — that is the lock on it.
Securityyour GitHub

Live read of your GitHub security posture: keys, OAuth apps, sessions.

  • Readable without the token, on purpose.
  • The one page worth checking on a phone.
03

Two regimes, two different jobs

The system is funded two ways over its life, and the right strategy is not the same in each. Written into the constitution on 2 October 2026 so the rule survives this conversation.

FREE — nowspread the load

Two uncapped, zero-retention seats. Nothing is scarce except attention and coverage, so the win comes from spreading work and stretching two seats.

  • Spread across both seats; never hammer one.
  • Use arena agents and extra sub-agents to stretch what two seats can do.
  • Keep everything current and shared — nothing is bought to patch a gap later.
  • A free seat can go quiet with no billing warning, so the probe board matters more here.
PAID — Go Plus and other subscriptionsefficiency and speed

Cost stops being the constraint and becomes the budget: daily, weekly and monthly limits. The optimisation inverts — efficiency and speed, not spreading.

  • Optimise for tokens per task and for latency.
  • LongCat becomes affordable, so slowness stops deciding the seat.
  • Rate limits become a real failure mode: budget, back off, queue.
  • Retention rules return with force — nothing that trains on prompts touches unreleased work, paid or not.
What never changesthe load-bearing rules

Evidence before claims, one agent to you, the boundaries on your stuff, and never marking my own work reviewed. A change of funding relaxes none of these.

  • Moving between regimes is a deliberate re-pin with the reason written down — never a side effect of a credit balance.
04

How you can spread the load

Ranked by how much they actually move the needle. The first one is recommended; the rest are optional. Written 2 October 2026.

1 · Name the next three outcomesbiggest lever

Not tasks — outcomes, in your words, in priority order. Everything else about how the work gets done is mine to figure out.

Why it is the biggest lever: right now I choose what to work on next, and a chosen priority is only ever as good as your intent that I do not have yet.

  • Three is enough. Ten is a wish list, and I will triage it against everything else.
  • "Make the console something I never need Zed for" is a complete instruction of that kind.
2 · Use the Drop box from your phonewhile you are out

Send a photo, a voice note or a sentence and it lands in front of me. The fastest way to add work without waiting for a session.

  • Good for "while you're out" instructions and for anything you see rather than remember.
3 · Open a second conversationparallel lines

Two threads means two lines of work in flight. Both free seats get used, which is exactly what the free regime is for.

  • One per subject, never one per question.
  • Not yet built into the console — see the honest gaps below.
4 · Ask for the arenawhen quality matters

Several agents attempt the same brief independently, and I synthesise the best result rather than averaging them.

  • Worth it for craft and judgement; wasteful for mechanical work.
  • Costs time, not money — the seats are free.
05

What you never need to do

Decide, approve or check the plumbinghandled
  • Which seat, which lane, how many workers, fast or thorough — my call, every time.
  • Commit, push, merge — mine, reported not asked.
  • Whether a change is verified — the gate decides, and a red gate blocks the push.
06

How a request actually travels

  1. You ask for something in Chat (or a lane is started for you).
  2. The harness reads the pin for that kind of work — the category.
  3. The category belongs to a lane: INTEL judges, OPS does the mechanics, DESIGN makes things.
  4. The harness calls the seat the pin names. If that seat is rate-limited, it retries on the fallback seat.
  5. A probe checks every pinned seat and every fallback seat is alive, on a timer.
  6. The board (Estate) reads the pins, the probes and the spend, and shows you which seat is on which lane.
